articles.title: Tom Brady, Didier Drogba, Rafael Nadal, Virat Kohli and Sergio Perez: E1 produces new wave of celebrity ownership in sport
articles.summary: History is made as the first all-electric speedboat race concludes in Jeddah, with the level of celebrity ownership in the series equally as ground-breaking
articles.body:
With a combined Instagram following of over 500 million, the line-up also includes global DJ Steve Aoki and Grammy-winning musician Marc Anthony.

From Hollywood descending on Wrexham, to Alpine attracting the likes of Rory McIlroy and Trent Alexander-Arnold to its investment group, the wave of celebrity ownership in sport is accelerating.

Star names bring further reach and financing to sports ventures.

But is this contribution always meaningful? Or more comparable to a rich boy's club?

E1's first event concluded in February, with Team Brady coming out on top, and Team Miami, owned by Anthony, in second.

This is not Anthony's first endeavour into sports ownership, becoming a minority stakeholder of NFL team Miami Dolphins in 2009 with his then wife Jennifer Lopez.

"When we first bought the Miami Dolphins, in the first seven years we knew that we were restructuring the team. I learnt that losing hurts when you're an owner of a team, it burns differently," said Anthony.

"It's about patience. It's about what you lose. It's what you learn by losing. That's what I realised, right? Every challenge is an opportunity.

"I told [my E1 pilots] no matter what happens just chalk it up to, 'oh, well I know how that feels and I don't want to feel it ever again'.

Drogba was also in Saudi Arabia to support his pilots, 10-time British Powerboat champion Oban Duncan and Kuwaiti jet-ski world champion Yousef Al Abdulrazzaq.

"First of all, we like to make history, and we are [going to] make it this weekend. It's the first time meeting my team, [I'm] so proud of it, so proud of them," said Drogba.

"I believe it's important to talk about inclusion, diversity, education, healthcare, that's what we're doing in Africa [with the Didier Drogba Foundation] and we really want to spread that message all around the world.

"We want to see how we can bring more eyes to the continent. Yes, I represent Ivory Coast, but I believe as a matter of fact, we also represent Africa. "

There are strong individual motivations behind each team owner's involvement in E1.

Aoki's father, Rocky Aoki, was a professional offshore powerboat racer. Despite numerous injury-inducing crashes and mechanical failures, Rocky was twice champion of the Benihana Grand Prix.

"[Powerboat racing] is a big part of my family history. It was a big part of my dad's life," said Aoki.

"I think that carried through, and when [E1] was a conversation on the table, if I have time, if I'm willing to put in X, Y and Z. I was all in.

"I have the opportunity to continue the legacy of my father. I'm not going to be driving it...he's crazier than me. I just have some of his drive and ambition, and his courage."

Former McLaren Motorsport business director and NASA consultant Rodi Basso is the co-founder and chief executive of E1. Basso joined forces with Formula E and Extreme E founder Alejandro Agag in lockdown to electrify racing on water.

Basso explained that each team owner was attracted to E1 due to its potential for growth, but also the small matter of legacy. "The other point is a bit more romantic," he said.

"They are all at the peak of their careers. Some of them are still ongoing with entertainment and sport. They wanted to have a project with a big impact.

"Rafa Nadal, before he listened to the E1 project, spoke to his managers and his team, and he said, 'when I stop playing, find me a project with high Impact'."

Professor Carlos Duarte is world-leading marine ecologist and E1's chief scientist.

"Now thanks to the relationship with E1, Carlos [Duarte] is working on a project to make the Academy of Rafa more sustainable," said Basso.

"Look at the due diligence in order to reduce the emissions and make it a more sustainable initiative, which is an incredible result of this relationship. That's what has been exchanged equally across all of [the team owners]."

E1 aims to promote gender equality, with each team consisting of one male and one female pilot. However, all eight team owners are men.

"This my biggest frustration, I can tell you that," said Basso.

"We tried. we tried very hard, and I cannot mention the name, but the same level of names. You can figure it out. Someone who is not playing anymore."

"First of all, we still have four teams to announce, because in the short-term, let's say four or five years, we want to keep it to 12 teams maximum, then we will see.

"I don't know. I don't have any answer, but I'm very keen to really understand and try again with the next four."

Like with all motorsport, winning is only possible through innovation.

E1's mission is to scale, but also to innovate technology that can be used in the real world.

"Not only do I love the water, not only was it a great opportunity to be a part of something so novel for the first time, and if you know anything about me, I'm one of those guys right, first through the door," said Anthony.

"I love the innovation. I love the message behind it. I believe that [E1] is the future."

Rodi Basso also detailed this ambition. "We take everything that we have learnt in motorsport and high-end automotive and we transfer it into the boat.

"Considering the gap in the culture of electrification there is in the marine industry, we have accelerated it by at least 15 years, with my boat, which we call the RaceBird."

Between E1's athlete team owners, there's seven Super Bowl titles, six Formula One Grand Prix wins, four Premier League titles, 22 tennis Grand Slams, and the ICC's male cricketer of the decade.

These men have won the biggest competitions on the globe, and this need to win has not faded.

"I'm highly competitive, even in my field," said Aoki.

"[I don't just] tour more than [any other] DJ, but any other music artists. Guinness Book of Records, most travelled music artist in one calendar year."

"You see the pedigrees of everyone else [who] has a team and they have astonishing records, but I'm glad that I'm in there because I don't want to be the underdog."

"[We're] fierce competitors, so we're going to build a strong team," said Drogba.

"We're inspired by legends such as Senna and Schumacher, but most especially by Lewis Hamilton, winning F1 championships, breaking barriers and acting as a leader for a new generation of pilots."

Sport gives celebrities the space to advocate for personal causes and have an impact on issues they care about.

But what ultimately ties each of these successful men together, and draws them to this new form of racing, is their desire for innovation, competition and legacy.

articles.title: World Athletics Championships: London misses out as Nairobi secures 2029 event | 'We are deeply disappointed'
articles.summary: The 2029 World Athletics Championships will be held in Nairobi, Kenya; it will be the first time the event has taken place in Africa; London's bid was unsuccessful, with UK Athletics CEO Jack Buckner saying: "We had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels"
articles.body:
Kenya has long been a superpower in distance running but has yet to host an event of this scale. The championships will return to Germany in 2031 with Munich hosting.

"We were fortunate to have four outstanding bids for 2029 and 2031, and this was not an easy decision for the council," said World Athletics president Sebastian Coe as he announced the decision following the Ultimate Championship in Hungary.

"The quality, ambition and commitment demonstrated by all four candidates underlines the strength and global appeal of the World Athletics Championships."

Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

"We would like to thank the Government, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Mayor of London and UK Sport for their fantastic support for our bid. Our thanks also to the London Stadium, West Ham United and our many stakeholders for their commitment and hard work to put the bid together.

"The UK is an incredible host for major sports events and the British public loves athletics. Athletic Ventures has the ambition to bring those events here and, although today's announcement hasn't gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world's athletes love competing here and we'll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.

"Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029."

Nairobi's selection represents a landmark moment for athletics, bringing its biggest global event to Africa for the first time.

"Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic," Coe said. "Athletics is woven into the fabric of Kenya."

After the new Ultimate Championship brought big cash prizes instead of medals for an invitation-only field of track's biggest names, it is back to the traditional worlds format next year in Beijing.

The World Championships run for 10 days, against three for the new Ultimate Championship, with a full slate of events. That means including competitions like the men's triple jump, shot put, walks and marathon which were not on the schedule in Budapest last week.

"Kenya is one of the great athletics nations. The sport is woven into the fabric of the country, and athletes such as world gold medallists Faith Kipyegon, Vivian Cheruiyot, Eliud Kipchoge, Hellen Obiri and David Rudisha, as well as two-time Olympic champion Kip Keino, multiple world cross-country champion Paul Tergat and multiple world half-marathon champion Tegla Loroupe, have shaped the history of our sport," Coe added.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment."

articles.title: Meet Mian Asghar Ali from Pakistan who planted over 5,700 trees around his small home just to make his mother smile again
articles.summary: Mian Asghar Ali's mother told him she wanted a garden full of greenery around their home, and he has planted nearly 5700 plants at his place!Some acts.
articles.body: Mian Asghar Ali's mother told him she wanted a garden full of greenery around their home, and he has planted nearly 5700 plants at his place!Some acts of love don't need grand gestures or big speeches. Sometimes, it is all about just actually listening when someone says what would make them happy, and then following through, even when it seems impossible at first. That's exactly what happened in a small town in Punjab, Pakistan, where a son’s response to his mother's simple wish slowly grew into something far bigger than either of them expected.Meet Mian Asghar Ali, who turned his mother's wish into a forest of over 5,700 treesMian Asghar Ali's mother told him she wanted a garden full of plants around their home. His first response wasn't encouraging. According to BBC Urdu, he explained that there simply wasn't enough room around the house to fit a garden, and turned down the idea.But his response did not turn out the way he expected. His mother didn't argue or retaliate much. She just went quiet, visibly let down. It was that silence, more than anything, which stayed with him. According to BBC Urdu, Ali said, "When I looked [back] at my mother's face, I felt a passion and urge." That single moment changed his mind completely.This hit Ali hard, and he decided to make it happen, even without much space to work with. He began planting in 2016, starting at a lower level and gradually filling every available inch around the house with greenery. What started as a modest attempt to please his mother slowly turned into an obsession with growing and caring for plants.Ali’s Marla house is now no less that na maini forestOver roughly a decade, Ali's six-marla home in Pattoki, Punjab, was transformed nealr into a miniature forest. He has now planted and personally maintained more than 5,700 trees on the property, which is an extraordinary number for how little land he had to begin with. He achieved this by using vertical space, courtyards, rooftops, and every unused corner around the home.None of this came free. Ali has spent nearly 14 lakh rupees on the project so far. That includes the cost of saplings, soil, tools, and the ongoing upkeep required to keep thousands of plants alive and healthy year-round.His motivation behind the story is applaudable; keeping his mother’s wish in mind, he transformed the home into a greenhouseLooking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: 'Would any politician feed this to their children?': CJP flags tents, maggots at Udaipur schools kitchen
articles.summary: JAIPUR: A Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) team led by co-convener Ashutosh Ranka inspected schools in villages of Udaipur district on Sunday as part of th.
articles.body: JAIPUR: A Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) team led by co-convener Ashutosh Ranka inspected schools in villages of Udaipur district on Sunday as part of the Adivasi School Thik Karo campaign and flagged poor infrastructure, unsafe buildings and lack of basic facilities.The team inspected primary schools in Demat, Pongli and Babari villages of Kherwara constituency. It said it found schools functioning out of makeshift tents and mud houses built by villagers after govt school buildings in the area were shut because they were dilapidated.CJP questioned how the tribal area development budget of Rs 1,500 crore was being spent if schools in the area were in such condition and local residents were being forced to pool funds to keep schools running and improve facilities."At the Govt Primary Tribal School in Demat, Kherwara (Udaipur), the message for Independence Day is still written on the wall. This is because no actual teaching has taken place for a whole month. The entire building is in a state of ruin. There is one teacher and two dilapidated classrooms for 70 children. We have completely abandoned our tribal children to the margins," Ranka said in a post on X.He added that a school in Demat village was operating out of a single mud room and food supplies were being stored inside a toilet.At another school inspected by the CJP team, members said they found maggots inside the kitchen where food was cooked for children."Would Madan Dilwar or Bhajan Lal Sharma feed their own children food from a kitchen infested with maggots like this? Would any politician from Rajasthan - or anywhere in the country - send their children to this school? So, why are the tribals forced to send their children to such schools?" Ranka said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news. articles.title: Meet the 24-year-old who saved up to £1,500 a month, bought two properties and built a growing property portfolio while living with his parents
articles.summary: Meet Jacob Waddington, a 24-year-old from Lancashire who has managed to build a property portfolio while many people his age are still trying to save .
articles.body: Meet Jacob Waddington, a 24-year-old from Lancashire who has managed to build a property portfolio while many people his age are still trying to save enough for their first home.The unusual part is not just his age. Since leaving college at 18, Waddington has been putting away as much as £1,000 a month, later increasing that to around £1,500 from a monthly salary of £2,200. He lived with his parents, kept his spending relatively low and eventually turned those savings into property.At 23, he and his girlfriend Holly bought a two-bedroom house for £98,000. A year later, they had another property, this time a 200-year-old cottage bought for £140,000.Meet Jacob WaddingtonWaddington started working for a telecommunications company after leaving college, earning £24,000 a year. Because he was still living at home and paid his parents around £200 a month, he was able to save a large part of his income.As his salary rose to £33,000, he was putting away about £1,500 a month.His lifestyle was relatively simple. He said he mainly spent money on going out at weekends, while he and Holly also enjoyed inexpensive activities such as walking and occasional meals out.The savings eventually gave the couple a different idea of what to do with their money.Instead of buying a home to live in, they bought one to renovateAs per LADBible, in May 2025, the couple considered buying a home together. But because neither was in a hurry to move out, they decided to buy a property that needed work, renovate it and potentially sell it.They paid £98,000 for a two-bedroom terraced house and put down a 25% deposit. They then spent about £20,000 renovating it.The work included a new kitchen, bathroom, boiler and replastered walls.By January 2026, around nine months after buying it, the renovation was finished. The property was then valued at £160,000.The first house became a rentalThe couple initially considered selling the renovated property but changed direction after seeing demand for rentals in the area.They remortgaged the house and rented it out in March 2026.The tenants pay £875 a month, while the couple's mortgage is around £430 a month, according to LADbible.That gave them another source of income while allowing them to keep the property.Then came the second houseThey bought a 200-year-old, one-bedroom cottage at the foot of Pendle Hill in Lancashire for £140,000.The historic location is associated with the Pendle witch trials, and the couple believes the rural setting could make it suitable for short-term holiday rentals.They plan to spend around £30,000 renovating the cottage and hope to eventually operate it as an Airbnb.Waddington estimates that if the property were rented for £120 a night at 60% occupancy, it could generate around £2,000 a month. After expenses including the mortgage, he estimates roughly £1,000 could remain.Those are his projections, rather than guaranteed returns.His approach is less about earning more and more about spending lessWaddington's story is interesting because his first step was not a high-paying investment strategy. It was saving consistently while his living costs were relatively low.His advice to other potential buyers is to consider properties that need work rather than automatically looking for a finished home.“Don't be afraid to buy something that needs a little work doing to it,” he said, arguing that a run-down property can offer room for its value to increase after renovation.The couple now plans to continue building their property portfolio before eventually buying a home for themselves.For Waddington, the journey that started with putting £1,000 aside each month at 18 has turned into something much bigger: by 24, he is already managing two properties and planning his next move.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: IIT-Bombay student suicide case: Institute apologises over earlier remarks; student affairs dean suspended
articles.summary: India News: MUMBAI: IIT-Bombay placed Prof Suryanarayana Doolla on immediate suspension from his deanship, following continued students' protests on campus for th.
articles.body: MUMBAI: IIT-Bombay placed Prof Suryanarayana Doolla on immediate suspension from his deanship, following continued students' protests on campus for the last three days. Prof Doolla was the dean of administrative affairs. He was accused of abetment of Sahil Wakode's death by suicide. Wakode's family also filed a case of harassment against him under the Atrocities Act. The institute issued a public apology on their social media handle, after students accused them of 'defaming' Wakode, without carrying out a detailed inquiry."We apologise for the statements contained in our earlier communication concerning the circumstances surrounding the unfortunate demise of Sahil," it said. "The details and circumstances leading up to the incident remain subject to investigation by the appropriate authorities. In view of the ongoing investigation, it was inappropriate to have set out or characterised details relating to the events preceding his demise before they had been duly established through the appropriate investigative process," the institute added. The administration also denied the allegations of the director's resignation, after videos of him from the protest went viral.In a mail sent to the campus residents, the institute director, Prof Shireesh Kedare, mentioned, 'the deanship of Prof Suryanarayan Doolla is suspended with immediate effect. Any further action will be taken after investigation'. Doolla has not been suspended from his professorship at the energy science and engineering department.A meeting of the institute's Board of Governors is underway.The students submitted a charter of 18 demands on Sunday night in a meeting with the director and the institute functionaries, which went on for three hours. The director signed the charter. Students pressed on the suspension of Prof Doolla and an apology along with 16 other demands.In the list of demands raised by the students' groups on the campus, the students have demanded an an independent investigation committee, with student representatives and external members recommended by students, suspension of officials who are found guilty after the investigation, a fair compensation for the families. Among the many demands, the students have also sought a code of conduct and sensitisation for professors.The director signed the list of demands on the live recording, though officials refused to comment. An open house with students is expected to be scheduled today.Protests erupted on the Powai campus on Friday night after Wakode, a second-year student of energy science and engineering, ended his life hours after he was caught using a mobile phone during the institute’s mid-semester examination. He allegedly uploaded the exam paper on an AI platform for answers. This is the third case of suicide on the campus this year.While the institute, in a statement, mentioned that no action was initiated against Wakode, many claimed that he was threatened with suspension.Also read: What are 18 demands of protesting students 'signed' by IIT Bombay directorGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Ontario couple paid C$200 for a landscape painting at a rural yard sale; six years later the work was identified as E J Hughes’s Lake Okanagan and sold at auction for C$402,500
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An Ontario couple who paid just C$200 for a landscape painting at a rural yard sale in 2001 later discovered that they had bought a work by renowned C.
articles.body: An Ontario couple who paid just C$200 for a landscape painting at a rural yard sale in 2001 later discovered that they had bought a work by renowned Canadian artist E J Hughes, literary weboste BC Booklook reported. Six years after the purchase, the painting, Lake Okanagan, was identified as a Hughes work and sold at auction for C$402,500.Hughes, a British Columbia painter's detailed landscapes have gained major value over the years. His work, once bought for a few hundred Canadian dollars, sells for hundreds of thousands and even millions at auction.Hughes is also the focus of a new documentary by Coquitlam filmmaker Jenn Strom. The Painted Life of E J Hughes looks at the artist’s life, his connection with British Columbia and the quiet way in which he worked. The documentary screened at the VIFF Centre in Vancouver in February.Strom became interested in Hughes while researching British Columbia’s history about seven years ago. Her research led her to the work of author Robert Amos, who wrote about Hughes and his life on Vancouver Island.Strom said she was drawn to the artist because his personality was very different from the public image often associated with artists. “He was humble and painfully shy. He didn’t have it in him to be out there promoting his own work,” Strom told Freshet News.Hughes’ as a war artistEdward John Hughes was born in North Vancouver on February 17, 1913, and grew up in Nanaimo and North Vancouver. During the Depression, he worked on fishing boats before studying at the Vancouver School of Decorative and Applied Art.One of his teachers was Frederick Varley, a member of Canada’s famous Group of Seven artists. Hughes also later co-founded a commercial art company with muralists Paul Goranson and Orville Fisher in 1934.When the Second World War began, Hughes enlisted with the Royal Canadian Artillery in 1939 and was posted to England. From 1943 to 1946, he worked as one of Canada’s official war artists.His wartime work included detailed drawings and paintings of military life. According to literary webiste BC BookLook, Hughes produced about 1,000 drawings and almost 30 complete paintings during his time as a war artist. Around 1,600 of his works are now held by the Canadian War Museum.His role required him to carefully record military equipment, uniforms, people and their surroundings. The detailed observation involved in that work later became an important part of his approach to painting landscapes.A quiet life on Vancouver IslandAfter returning to the West Coast in 1946, Hughes settled at Shawnigan Lake with his wife, Fern. Strom filmed the area and the home where the artist lived while making her documentary. “He needed silence. Peace and quiet,” Strom said.Hughes spent much of his career focusing on the landscapes of British Columbia. He was deeply interested in nature and in recording places with careful detail.“I feel that, when I am doing my painting, it is a form of worship,” Hughes said in a 1961 CBC television production.Hughes had also considered whether to focus more on figures or landscapes, but eventually chose landscapes because he felt they represented the British Columbia and Canadian environment strongly and would sell more readily.Despite his growing reputation, he struggled financially at one stage and nearly gave up painting. His career received important support from art dealer Max Stern, who had previously represented Emily Carr.Stern tracked Hughes down at Shawnigan Lake in 1951 after receiving advice from Lawren Harris, a founding member of Canada’s Group of Seven. He later recalled meeting a shy artist who was not fully aware of the quality of his own work. Stern decided to represent him.After their first meeting, Stern bought all the work then available in Hughes’ studio for $500. The relationship helped Hughes build a stronger career while also giving him support in dealing with the public and the art market.From C$200 yard sale find to millionsThe value of Hughes’ work increased significantly as his reputation grew. His painting Lake Okanagan is one of the most striking examples. Bought at an Ontario yard sale for C$200 in 2001, it was sold for C$402,500, six years later.The price was part of a wider rise in the value of Hughes’ paintings. BC BookLook noted that Rivers Inlet sold for $920,000 in 2005, then the highest price paid for a work by a living Canadian artist.Other works have reached even higher prices. Hughes’ Fishboats, River Inlet sold for $2 million at Heffel Auction. In November 2025, his 1949 painting Entrance to Howe Sound sold for $4.8 million.Strom said Hughes’ story continues to attract attention because of the strength of his work and the contrast between his quiet personality and the growing value of his paintings. “His story keeps growing,” she said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: When a district in Florida used robot rabbits to eliminate growing population of Burmese pythons and protect Everglades
articles.summary: Tech News News: Florida used an unusual tool to control the growing population of invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades: solar-powered robot rabbits. In 2025, th.
articles.body: Florida used an unusual tool to control the growing population of invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades: solar-powered robot rabbits. In 2025, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida teamed up to deploy robotic rabbit decoys designed to mimic real prey and lure pythons out of hiding using artificial intelligence (AI), heat signatures and scent simulation.The robots are part of Florida’s broader effort to remove Burmese pythons, which have disrupted native wildlife populations across the state. The devices use AI-powered cameras to detect approaching snakes and alert officials, who can then send trained python removal agents to capture and remove them. The technology is being used alongside the annual Florida Python Challenge and other removal programmes, not replacing them.​How Florida’s AI-powered robot rabbits work​The solar-powered robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent intended to attract the snakes, which use thermal sensing and smell while hunting. Each robot has an AI-powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts South Florida Water Management District officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.The district and University of Florida are deploying the robots at sites across South Florida where pythons are known to hide. The approach is intended to help monitor areas that can be difficult to survey using conventional methods.​“These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,” the district noted.​Why Florida is targeting Burmese pythons​Burmese pythons were introduced into the Everglades during the 1970s and have since become an invasive predator in Florida. Researchers estimate that between 100,000 and 300,000 Burmese pythons are present across the state’s subtropical regions. The snakes can grow longer than 18 feet, and adult females can lay more than 70 eggs in a single clutch. Their presence has affected native mammals, birds and reptiles, reducing available prey for species including Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.​A 2012 US Geological Survey study found that raccoon and opossum populations in parts of the Everglades had declined by nearly 99% following the spread of Burmese pythons.​Florida Python Challenge adds to python removal efforts​Florida has also relied on trained contractors and public participation to remove Burmese pythons. The annual Florida Python Challenge brings professional and amateur hunters together for a 10-day competition, and participants must complete a safety course before taking part. In the 2026 challenge, 907 participants from 30 states, as well as Vietnam and Canada, collectively removed 280 Burmese pythons. The competition's overall tally has now exceeded 1,600 snakes.Tom Rahill won the $10,000 grand prize after removing 96 snakes, while Rahm Levinson received $1,000 for capturing the longest python, measuring 16 feet, five inches. Additional prizes were awarded across professional, novice and military categories.​“The number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades during the 2026 Florida Python Challenge is a major victory for Florida’s native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation,” FWC chairman Rodney Barreto said in a statement.Since 2017, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and South Florida Water Management District contractors have removed more than 19,000 snakes. The district's robotic rabbit programme is intended to add another method to those ongoing efforts.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Meet 'Little Einstein' Laurent Simons: 16-year-old PhD holder who is now researching how to slow human ageing and extend lifespan
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At 15, most teenagers are preparing for higher secondary examinations or thinking about university. Laurent Simons was already defending a doctoral th.
articles.body: At 15, most teenagers are preparing for higher secondary examinations or thinking about university. Laurent Simons was already defending a doctoral thesis in theoretical quantum physics. The Belgian researcher completed his first PhD at the University of Antwerp in November 2025, aged 15. Simons' academic journey had begun years earlier. Long before his PhD, he had become internationally known as a child who moved through formal education at an unusually fast pace. Now, his research interests have moved beyond quantum physics. He is pursuing another doctorate connected to medical science and artificial intelligence, with an interest in understanding ageing and extending human life.His academic journey began unusually earlySimons (now 16) was born in Belgium and attracted attention as a young child because of his ability to absorb academic material quickly. According to Dutch news broadcaster NOS, he started primary school at the age of two. In 2018, Simons began studying electrical engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. At nine, he was already working on university-level material. As reported by Reuters in November 2019, he was working on a brain-on-a-chip project, which combined electrical engineering and biomedical research. The project involved placing neurons and making connections to examine their responses to medication.At the time, Simons said that he wanted to pursue a PhD and also study medicine. He did not complete the Eindhoven programme. A disagreement developed between his family and the university over the timetable for completing the course, and he left the programme in 2019. Simons moved to the University of Antwerp, where he changed his academic focus to physics.He completed a physics bachelor's degree at 11In July 2021, at the age of 11, Simons completed a bachelor's degree in physics at the University of Antwerp. He then completed his master's degree in quantum physics at the University of Antwerp at age 12. Simons completed the master's in about a year, passing his exams in his first semester before completing his thesis and internship in Germany. At the time, Simons said that he eventually wanted to work as a scientist and develop artificial organs. That ambition was connected to his interest in medicine and the human body. The next step was further research in physics. His research interests have repeatedly crossed traditional academic boundaries. In 2019, when he was nine, Simons was already interested in combining engineering and medicine through brain-on-a-chip research.He also gained research experience in Germany. As per the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics, after his bachelor's degree, Simons joined the attoworld team at LMU Munich and the institute for an internship.He defended his PhD at 15His first doctorate took him deep into theoretical quantum physics. According to the University of Antwerp's official website, his research dealt with Bose-Einstein condensates, ultracold bosonic gases and polarons. On November 17, 2025, Simons defended his doctoral thesis at the University of Antwerp. His achievement attracted international attention because of his age, but his academic record by then included university degrees, research experience and published work.His next question is much closer to human biologyAfter quantum physics, Simons turned his attention to medicine and artificial intelligence. Recent reports say he began work on a second doctoral project in medical science, involving AI and biomedical research. As reported by Norwegian newspaper VG, he is working on a medical doctorate at the Helmholtz Centre in Munich, Germany. He also has an interest in using science and technology to extend human life. As per a 2026 report from The Brighter Side of News, his grandparents had cardiovascular diseases. He described death as “a huge puzzle with many pieces from many different fields.” He said those fields include biology, medicine, engineering and physics, and added, “My mission is to help put all of those pieces together.”An expected high IQOne of the details that attracted attention when Simons was a child was his reported IQ. TAs per the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics website, scientists had assessed him as having an IQ of at least 145. The institute also noted that an IQ above 130 is generally considered to fall within the highly gifted range. Simons’ life is not entirely centred on laboratories and university classrooms. Norwegian academic newspaper Khrono reported that Simons enjoys spending time with friends, playing Fortnite and Clash Royale, going go-karting, watching action films with his family and going to restaurants.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: North Korea defies sanctions push, rejects report on overseas workers and nuclear funding
articles.summary: Rest of World News: North Korea has rejected international efforts to tighten enforcement of sanctions against it, saying such measures cannot stop the country's developm.
articles.body: North Korea has rejected international efforts to tighten enforcement of sanctions against it, saying such measures cannot stop the country's development or prevent it from defending what it calls its core interests, state media KCNA reported on Monday.According to Reuters, the statement came from a North Korean foreign ministry spokesperson, who accused the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) of fabricating a report aimed at portraying what Pyongyang described as normal and mutually beneficial economic cooperation with other countries as illegal.The MSMT, an 11-country group that monitors violations and evasion of UN sanctions, said in a report issued on September 16 that North Korea continued to send workers overseas in breach of UN Security Council resolutions.The group estimated that the workers generated between $450 million and $800 million in 2025, potentially providing revenue for North Korea's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes."The DPRK's relations of exchange and cooperation with other countries cannot be subject to interference or investigation of a third party," a North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a statement. Pyongyang described its overseas economic activities as legitimate cooperation under bilateral and multilateral agreements.Reuters reported that the MSMT estimated between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers remained active in at least 17 countries, mainly China and Russia. The group called on countries to enforce UN resolutions by repatriating North Korean workers and refusing to issue them new work permits.Sanctions on North KoreaThe United Nations sanctions regime against North Korea was first imposed in 2006 after Pyongyang's nuclear test. Since then, the UN Security Council has adopted a series of resolutions expanding restrictions in response to North Korea's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes.The sanctions cover a broad range of military and economic activities. They include an arms embargo, restrictions on the transfer of nuclear and missile-related technology and assistance, asset freezes and travel bans on designated individuals and entities, and restrictions on financial services and banking relationships linked to North Korea.The measures have also targeted North Korea's sources of foreign currency by banning or restricting exports of commodities including coal, iron, iron ore, seafood, lead, copper, nickel, silver and zinc. The sanctions also place limits on North Korea's access to crude oil and refined petroleum products and restrict shipping and the transportation of prohibited goods.The sanctions further restrict joint ventures, investment and certain forms of technical and scientific cooperation with North Korean entities. Countries are also required to take action against vessels and companies involved in sanctions evasion and the movement of prohibited goods.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2013, Canadian teenager Ann Makosinski invented a flashlight powered by body heat; now she is creating colourful toys to teach children about renewable energy
articles.summary: Rest of World News: They say some children are born prodigies, and when it comes to Ann Makosinski, the statement holds true. As a teenager living in Canada, her friend l.
articles.body: They say some children are born prodigies, and when it comes to Ann Makosinski, the statement holds true. As a teenager living in Canada, her friend living in the Philippines told her that she couldn't study at night since her family couldn't afford electricity to turn the lights on. Soon she wondered if there was a way to have light without traditional electricity. This is when she came up with a record-making invention, a flashlight powered by body heat.Like other children her age, Makosinski did not watch television or play video games. She spent her time listening to the opera, watching silent movies and learning to play the piano and violin. Interestingly, her first toy was a box of transistors. “I wasn’t given many toys, so I had to make my own,” she said to CNN back in 2019. “I would take garbage and my hot glue gun from around the house and piece together these so-called inventions, and obviously they never worked, but the idea of taking things from around me and piecing them together to make something better just kind of came really naturally.”A new kind of lightMakosinski was only 15 when she invented a flashlight that was powered by the heat of the user's hands. The Hollow Flashlight uses thermoelectric technology to convert the temperature difference between the user's hand and the surrounding air into electricity. The device uses Peltier tiles, which generate electricity when one side is heated by the palm of the hand and the other is cooled.No batteries are required, with the flashlight running entirely on human body heat that would otherwise go to waste. School students, therefore, could study without worrying about running out of battery power.The Hollow Flashlight earned Makosinski a win in the 15-16 age category at the 2013 Google Science Fair and won at the 2014 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair. Her wins made her an international media sensation. She made appearances on shows such as 'The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon' and was featured in publications such as TIME and Forbes. She even gave a TEDxTeen Talk titled 'Why I don't use a smartphone'. Makosinski only bought her first phone, an old-fashioned flip model, at the age of 18.eDrink: A mug that generates electricityThe intrigued teenager did not stop there. Soon, she launched her next major invention, the eDrink. At 18, while enrolled at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, she designed a coffee mug to capture the excess heat from a hot beverage and convert it into electricity. This excess energy could then be used to provide a small charge to a phone or other device for 30 minutes. It uses Peltier tiles (thermoelectric generators), and by heating one side of the tiles with your drink and cooling the other side with the design of the mug (and a bunch of electronic circuits, of course), electricity is produced."I got the inspiration for my project when I noticed that my high school friends were always complaining about their phones dying too soon and that their coffee was too hot to drink," she told Society for Science.Toys with renewable energyNow 29, Makosinski is looking to inspire other young girls across the world to use their minds and creativity in a similar fashion. Her interest in thermoelectric technology has led her toward a different kind of invention: toys designed to teach children about renewable energy.She has created bright-coloured toys that help kids learn about renewable energy in exciting ways. They can see and play with it as it lights up, spins or makes sound when powered by sunlight, water or a hand-wound mechanism.The goal now, she told CNN, is to have other youngsters, girls in particular, follow her into the world of science.“I just want, especially young kids, to feel like they can invent their own solutions and they don’t have to wait for other people to make them,” said Makosinski, who described herself as “a normal girl who just used her time differently after school.”“I want to inspire people to be more creative with the resources they have around them,” she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An Australian caver spotted an 11-km scar while searching Google Earth; scientists later found a tornado had torn through the Nullarbor
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An unusual line across the otherwise open landscape of Australia’s Nullarbor Plain might have gone unnoticed if not for a caver looking at satellite i.
articles.body: An unusual line across the otherwise open landscape of Australia’s Nullarbor Plain might have gone unnoticed if not for a caver looking at satellite imagery. While browsing Google Earth, he came across a long, narrow disturbance cutting through the remote terrain. There were no buildings nearby, no obvious roads and no reports of a storm that could explain it. From above, the feature looked remarkably clear. It stretched for about 11 kilometres, crossing the border between Western Australia and South Australia. Months later, scientists examining the site and comparing older satellite images reached an explanation.An Australian caver spotted the mysterious scar on Google EarthSatellite images showed a scar between roughly 160 and 250 metres across, extending for kilometres through the dry landscape. Its position also helped explain why the discovery took time. The scar is about 22 kilometres north of the Trans-Australian Railway and roughly 90 kilometres east-northeast of Forrest, a former railway settlement. There is very little regular human activity across the surrounding country, meaning a weather event could pass through without anyone nearby to report it.The researcher used satellite imagery from different dates to establish when the change had appeared. According to the study published in the Journal of Southern Hemisphere Earth Systems Science, titled ‘Tornado scar on the Nullarbor Plain, Australia’, their comparison placed the formation of the scar between 16 and 18 November 2022. Around the same period, several circular blue areas could be seen in the imagery. These were interpreted as temporary pools produced by heavy rainfall.Physical evidence linked the scar to a powerful stormThe scar itself was only part of the evidence. Looking at images taken before and after the suspected event allowed the team to determine that the feature had not always been present. Weather information from the same period pointed to a storm system moving across the region. The rainfall and cloud cover provided a plausible setting for the ground disturbance, but they did not by themselves establish that a tornado had passed over the Nullarbor.When researcher eventually examined the area, they found curved, cycloidal traces running along sections of the scar. Such marks are associated with the movement of debris and vegetation within tornado damage paths. Their presence gave the otherwise puzzling satellite feature a much more specific explanation.What the unusual marks revealedThe shape of the disturbance suggested that the storm had not simply produced widespread flooding or surface runoff. Cycloidal marks were visible in parts of the affected area, while the scar showed erosion and the removal of soil and pieces of vegetation.According to ABC News, Dr John Allen, a meteorologist at Central Michigan University who was not involved in the research, pointed, "Cycloidal marks are quite evident, and these are seen in US tornado damage paths.”"The appearance of the path without substantive evidence of flooding as an alternative cause would further lend support to this argument."The study estimated that the tornado may have reached F2 to F3 intensity, with estimated wind speeds of more than 200 km/h. Its track indicated movement from west to east, with clockwise rotation. The researcher estimated that it may have remained on the ground for between seven and 13 minutes.Australia’s remote Nullarbor left the tornado unseenThe lack of eyewitness accounts is less surprising when the location is considered. The Nullarbor Plain contains enormous areas of sparsely populated, largely flat terrain. The tornado did not cross a town or strike major infrastructure, so there was little chance of someone seeing it directly or reporting damage immediately afterwards.The researcher noted that only three tornadoes had previously been recorded in the region. All three occurred during November, the same month as the event identified from the satellite imagery.That does not establish a broader seasonal pattern on its own, particularly in an area where observations are limited. It does, however, provide an interesting point of comparison for a region with relatively little historical tornado documentation.The scar remained visible long after the stormThe dry conditions of the Nullarbor also helped preserve the evidence. The disturbance could still be seen around 18 months after the suspected tornado. In a landscape where vegetation recovery is slow, the damaged strip did not quickly disappear beneath new growth.That persistence gave scientists an opportunity that would not necessarily exist in a wetter or more heavily vegetated environment. A storm that had passed without witnesses had effectively left a record of its route on the ground.Matej Lipar, a physical geographer from the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts and a study author, described the feature as a kind of surface signature left behind by the storm. With comparatively little vegetation covering the ground, the path remained visible long after the weather event itself had ended.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Egyptian archaeologists uncovered rare rock-cut tombs at an ancient Nile Delta site, with Roman camp remains found in the layers above
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Archaeologists working at the ancient Tell el-Yahudiya site in Egypt's Qalyubia governorate have uncovered several rock-cut tombs, while continuing to.
articles.body: Archaeologists working at the ancient Tell el-Yahudiya site in Egypt's Qalyubia governorate have uncovered several rock-cut tombs, while continuing to uncover remains of a Roman camp. The discoveries were made by an Egyptian archaeological mission during continued excavation work at the site. Evidence indicates that the burials date from the late New Kingdom and continued into the Late Period.The Roman camp remains were found in the upper layers above the rock-cut tombs, indicating that the site continued to be used in later periods. The Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities reveals that the tombs are particularly notable because rock-cut burials are uncommon in the Nile Delta, where clay-rich soil is widespread.What are the two types of rock-cut tombs found at Tell el-YahudiyaThe tombs were built in different ways, with two distinct architectural designs identified during the excavation. In one type, the entrance begins with a staircase leading to a hall lined with burial openings (known as bayatat). The other type consists of a rectangular shaft that leads to two burial chambers. The Ministry notes that these varied designs are significant because rock-cut tombs are relatively uncommon in the Nile Delta. The Delta's clay soil explains the rarity of this type of tomb. Finding tombs carved into rock here is important for understanding burial patterns and how they developed in the eastern Delta over the ages.How did archaeologists determine the age of the newly discovered tombsArchaeological objects found in the tombs helped the mission determine when they were used. The evidence shows that the tombs date to the late New Kingdom and continued to be used during the Late Period. This indicates that the burial area remained in use across different periods of ancient Egyptian history.The finds were portable artifacts associated with the tombs, and they helped determine the periods in which the tombs were used. This reflects funerary activity in the region extending across successive historical periods.What does the Roman camp reveal about Tell el-YahudiyaThe mission is also completing the uncovering of the Roman camp remains in the surface layers above the tombs. The remains were found above the rock-cut tombs, showing that the area continued to be used after the earlier burials. The Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said the Roman remains add another layer to the history of Tell el-Yahudiya. The site was mainly associated with the Hyksos period and once contained a large camp from that time. It was later used during the Greek and Roman periods. The discovery of both tombs and camp remains indicates that the same area served different purposes over several historical periods.How did Tell el-Yahudiya change over different historical periodsThe site was already an important location during the Hyksos period, when the area contained a large camp. It was later used during the Greek and Roman periods. The newly uncovered tombs and Roman camp remains provide further evidence of this continued use. The discovery is also notable because rock-cut tombs are relatively uncommon in the Nile Delta.The ministry noted similar examples at Kom El-Shoqafa in Alexandria and in parts of the northern coast. At Tell el-Yahudiya, the archaeological layers now contain evidence of both burial activity and later use as a camp. The mission is continuing its work to uncover the remains of the Roman camp.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ram Temple donations 'theft' case: SIT to file first chargesheet on or before September 25
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court-appointed Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the alleged theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya will file .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court-appointed Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the alleged theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya will file its first chargesheet in the case on or before September 25, a CJI-led bench was informed on Monday.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the bench that the chargesheet would have to be filed as the statutory 90-day period from the first arrest in the case would lapse soon.“Ninety days from the date of the first arrest are going to be over on September 25, so we will have to file the chargesheet, otherwise, they (the accused) will get default bail,” Mehta said.The bench, comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, also perused a detailed status report submitted by the SIT in a sealed cover.Under Section 167(2) of the CrPC, an accused becomes entitled to statutory bail if the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet in the trial court within the stipulated period of 60 or 90 days.The bench had earlier directed the probe team to complete its investigation expeditiously and take it to its logical conclusion. It had also asked the SIT to file a status report in a sealed cover on the progress of the probe into the alleged theft of donations.The Supreme court had taken note of the formation of a four-member SIT headed by IGP Kiran S to investigate the alleged embezzlement of donations and directed the Uttar Pradesh government to include a forensic auditor in the probe team.Observing that “remedial actions will have to be taken”, the bench had said steps would be taken to “ensure transparency” and directed the SIT to submit a status report.The court's directions came after allegations of irregularities surfaced in the management of donations at the Ram Temple. Several petitioners approached the Supreme Court seeking a CBI probe and a forensic audit of the temple trust’s finances.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2018, Jon Bon Jovi paid $10 million for a Palm Beach home, demolished it and rebuilt; two years later he sold the new mansion for $19.85 million and bought a $43 million estate
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Rock star Jon Bon Jovi made a quick multi-million-pound property deal in South Florida, selling a newly built oceanfront mansion in Palm Beach for $19.
articles.body: Rock star Jon Bon Jovi made a quick multi-million-pound property deal in South Florida, selling a newly built oceanfront mansion in Palm Beach for $19.85 million (£15.8 million), just two years after buying the original property for about half that amount. According to property records and local real estate reports, first detailed by The Real Deal, the musician completed the sale of the custom-built home on North Ocean Boulevard in July 2020. On the same day, he bought a much larger oceanfront estate farther south on South Ocean Boulevard for $43 million (£34.2 million). The two deals represent one of the fastest and most profitable residential redevelopments by a celebrity in Palm Beach in recent years.A $10 million property makeoverBon Jovi bought the original property at 1075 North Ocean Boulevard in 2018 through a limited liability company for $10 million. Instead of moving into the existing 1950s house, the singer decided to demolish it. He then built a custom two-storey mansion covering about 5,000 square feet. The home was designed in a modern Mediterranean style. The finished property has five bedrooms, five full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms. It also includes an oceanfront swimming pool, a covered loggia, a courtyard, an elevator and a two-car garage. Yahoo News reported that the property was initially listed for $22.9 million before the asking price was reduced. The final sale price of $19.85 million gave Bon Jovi a large gross gain compared with the original $10 million land purchase, although construction costs would have reduced the overall profit.Moving to a larger estateInstead of keeping the property or using the proceeds elsewhere, Jon Bon Jovi immediately put the money into a much larger Palm Beach estate. Records show that he bought 1020 South Ocean Boulevard on the same day the North Ocean Boulevard property was sold. The seller was a company linked to real estate developer and trial attorney Thomas Holofcener. The new estate sits on more than one acre of land and has much more living space. The mansion covers more than 10,000 square feet and includes seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and five half-bathrooms. Built in 2007, the home has several luxury features, including a courtyard, swimming pool, wine cellar, full home gym and a separate apartment for staff. It also has direct beach access across the street, making it especially attractive in Palm Beach’s luxury property market.Palm Beach’s property boomThe two transactions also show how strong South Florida’s luxury property market was in 2020. Wealthy buyers, especially from New York and New Jersey, increasingly looked to Florida for primary and second homes because of its tax advantages and warm climate. Palm Beach was one of the areas that saw strong sales and rising property prices during 2020. High-end buyers were purchasing land, renovating older homes and tearing down existing properties to build new custom oceanfront estates. Jon Bon Jovi is one of several well-known public figures who have invested in property in the area, joining other wealthy homeowners in the exclusive beachfront community. The buyer of Bon Jovi’s North Ocean Boulevard home was not publicly identified in property records. The sale was completed through a trustee account.Holdouts against mega-assemblagesIn mid-2025, reports from Realtor.com and The Wall Street Journal said that Bon Jovi’s $43 million estate on South Ocean Boulevard had become a key target in a major land-buying effort. A mystery buyer, reportedly linked to tech billionaires, spent more than $250 million buying nearby properties. This included an adjacent 2.8-acre oceanfront plot bought from cosmetics heir William Lauder for about $178 million. According to industry reports, Bon Jovi repeatedly turned down multi-million-dollar offers to sell his property. He chose to keep his 10,000-square-foot estate despite strong pressure to sell as buyers continued assembling large amounts of land in the area.Billionaires’ Row expansionsKen Griffin (Citadel): The hedge fund founder has acquired more than 27 connected acres along South County Road in Palm Beach. He has spent well over $350 million on several mansions and oceanfront properties, including the historic $105 million La Follia estate. His purchases are intended to create one of the largest private residential compounds in U.S. history.William Lauder: The Estée Lauder heir spent more than $25 million in 2020 buying neighboring properties on North Ocean Boulevard. He demolished the existing homes and later offered the combined property for between $178 million and $200 million.Broader South Florida celebrity relocationsBilly Joel: In late 2024, the musician completed the sale of his large oceanfront estate in Manalapan for $42.6 million. He later bought a $40 million waterfront home in Boca Raton’s Sanctuary community.Mark Wahlberg: After selling his $63 million Beverly Hills mansion, Wahlberg bought a $37 million estate at Stone Creek Ranch in Delray Beach.Kevin James: The actor purchased a $17.15 million custom-built home in Boca Raton’s Royal Palm Yacht & Country Club. His move reflects the growing interest among high-profile buyers in private, gated communities across South Florida.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.
